title: Amitabha
hook: Buddha of Infinite Light and Infinite Life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the primal vow: entrusting, wishing, the name, and a door the sutra says is already open. Your line: the primal vow.

A gilded figure seated on a temple altar in Japan, hands in the lap, fingers and thumbs forming two small circles. A tall standing figure in a Chinese hall, one hand raised, the other lowered and open, as if reaching down to someone. A small paper image taped above a bed in a nursing home. Three images, one Buddha. In Japan he's Amida. In China, Amituofo. In the Sanskrit sutras he carries two names, and today's word is the first: Amitabha.
screen: `A SEATED FIGURE IN JAPAN.` → `A HAND REACHING DOWN.` → `AMITABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the two names, which the short sutra explains itself. You heard part of this with Honen; here's the whole. Why is that Buddha called Amitabha? Because his light is measureless, shining without obstruction over the Buddha-lands in every direction. And why Amitayus? Because his life, and the life of the people in his land, is measureless too. Amitabha, infinite light. Amitayus, infinite life. The Japanese Amida holds both. Second, who he is: the monk from two days ago. The longer sutra says Dharmakara kept his vows, became a Buddha, and lives now in the land of bliss. So every time someone says his name, they name a vow kept. Third, the light: without obstruction. Sunlight on a city doesn't pick which roofs to land on, and in the sutra Amitabha's light reaches every land, near and far. One clarification, since the shops confuse it: Amitabha isn't the laughing, round-bellied figure in gift shops. That's Budai, Hotei in Japan, a different figure altogether. Fourth, how people meet him: through images like these, through the name in Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese, and, the short sutra says, at the end of life, when he appears with a holy company before a dying person who has held his name in mind. Some readers see that welcome in the standing statue's lowered hand.
screen: `TWO NAMES: LIGHT AND LIFE.` · `DHARMAKARA, A VOW KEPT.` · `LIGHT WITHOUT OBSTRUCTION.` · `THE HAND REACHING DOWN.` · then, large: `INFINITE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture a small, warm light in the center of your chest, the size of a candle flame, and with each out-breath let it grow: your body, the room, the street, the city. Let it spread until it has no edge and nothing blocks it, not walls, not distance, not anyone's past, and rest there, breathing.
Amitabha. The Buddha of infinite light, also called Amitayus, infinite life: Amida in Japan, Amituofo in China, the monk Dharmakara with his vows fulfilled. Today's word.
Your line: infinite light. A name that means a vow kept, shining in every direction. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists keep images of Amitabha, seated or standing with one hand lowered in welcome, on temple and home altars, and call his name as Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra, and the Buddha asks you why that Buddha is called Amitabha. what's the sutra's answer?
options: because his land lies in the west.
because his light is measureless and shines without obstruction.
because he was once a king.
fork.reveal: the short sutra gives the reason itself: measureless light, unobstructed in every direction. measureless life gives him his second name, Amitayus.

original.note: Sanskrit: Amitabha, infinite light. his second name, Amitayus (अमितायुस्), means infinite life. Japanese Amida (阿弥陀).

chat.says: Is Amitabha the laughing, round-bellied Buddha I see in gift shops?
options: No, that's Budai. Amitabha is the Buddha of infinite light and infinite life.
Yes, the big belly stands for the infinite life his name promises.
Yes, he's how the Buddha Shakyamuni is shown in Japan and China.
chat.meaning: The laughing figure is Budai, Hotei in Japan. Amitabha means infinite light; he's also called Amitayus, infinite life: Dharmakara with his vows fulfilled.

Amitabha.meaning: infinite light: the Buddha of the land of bliss

Amida.meaning: his name in Japan, holding both light and life

Budai.meaning: the laughing, round-bellied figure; Hotei in Japan

Dharmakara.meaning: the monk whose vows were fulfilled when he became Amitabha

sources.ref: Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha (why he is called Amitabha and Amitayus; his appearing at the end of life)

notes: The two names are explained from the Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha's own words (paraphrased); in some versions of the sutra both explanations appear under the name Amitayus/Amitabha in slightly different order. Confirm.
Image descriptions (seated figure with meditation mudra; standing figure with one hand lowered) are general; confirm the lowered hand as a gesture of welcome (raigo).
Budai/Hotei distinction: confirm wording is respectful to both.
Japanese Amida (阿弥陀) and Sanskrit Amitayus spelling in Devanagari (अमितायुस्): confirm.
